w: Built for forced labour, not mass murder, this camp on Lublin's outskirts became one of the largest in the Nazi system, with three gas chambers and 227 structures. An estimated 78,000 people were murdered here in Operation Reinhard. The Red Army's rapid 1944 advance caught the SS off guard, seizing it nearly intact.
s: The death camp the Nazis had no time to destroy
_facts: Nazi concentration and extermination camp on Lublin's outskirts, operated October 1941 to July 1944
Around 227 structures, three gas chambers, two wooden gallows
Estimated 78,000 people murdered during Operation Reinhard
Captured nearly intact by the Red Army in July 1944 due to the speed of Operation Bagration

w: One of the oldest royal residences preserved anywhere in Poland began under Duke Casimir II the Just, centuries before the Gothic Revival makeover of the 1800s gave it the turreted look it wears now. The castle sits right against the Old Town, having outlasted the medieval city that grew up around it.
s: One of Poland's oldest royal residences, redisguised
_facts: Medieval castle established by High Duke Casimir II the Just
One of the oldest preserved royal residencies in Poland
Its Gothic Revival appearance is due to a 19th-century reconstruction

w: Jesuits built this cathedral between 1592 and 1617 on a model borrowed from Rome's Chiesa del Gesu, one of Poland's first Baroque churches. It only picked up cathedral status in the early 19th century, and has served as Lublin's archdiocesan seat since 1992 - a Roman design settling into a Polish role.
s: One of Poland's first Baroque churches, modelled on Rome
_facts: Built 1592-1617 as a Jesuit church, modelled on the Chiesa del Gesù in Rome
One of the first Baroque churches built in Poland
Designated cathedral in the early 19th century; archdiocesan cathedral since 1992

w: Walled in on a hill overlooking the Old Town since the 17th century, this cemetery sits on a former medieval fortress site and holds some of the last physical evidence of centuries of Jewish life in Lublin. The high perimeter wall that once enclosed it today just as effectively keeps the modern city at a distance.
s: The last physical trace of Jewish Lublin, walled since 1600s
_facts: Located on a hill between Kalinowszczyzna and Sienna Streets, overlooking the Old Town
Enclosed by a 17th-century wall; sits on the site of a former medieval fortress
Provides some of the last surviving physical evidence of Lublin's historic Jewish community

w: Raised in the 14th century under Casimir III the Great, this Gothic tower is the last significant survivor of Lublin's medieval city walls, and once marked the start of the road to Krakow. A trumpeter's post and clock were fitted into it later, giving a defensive structure a second life as a civic timekeeper.
s: The last standing gate of Lublin's medieval walls
_facts: Gothic city gate built in the 14th century under King Casimir III the Great
One of the last remaining components of Lublin's original city walls
Marked the route toward Kraków; later fitted with a trumpeter's post and a clock

w: Completed in 1930 in a mix of Classical Revival and Art Deco, this synagogue and yeshiva once anchored one of the most renowned centres of Talmudic study in prewar Europe, drawing rabbinical students from across the continent. It survives on Lubartowska Street as a rare link to that vanished world of Jewish Lublin.
s: A once-famous yeshiva, built in Art Deco style
_facts: Hasidic synagogue and yeshiva at 85 Lubartowska Street
Designed by Agenor Smoluchowski, mixing Classical Revival and Art Deco styles
Completed 1930

w: Known historically as the Jewish Gate, this passage once marked the physical border between Lublin's Christian and Jewish quarters. Today it houses a cultural centre built around remembering that vanished Polish-Jewish city, running the arts and education programmes that keep the memory of that border alive.
s: The old gate between Lublin's Christian and Jewish quarters
_facts: Also known as the Jewish Gate; historically the passage between the Christian and Jewish parts of Lublin
Now houses the Grodzka Gate - NN Theatre Centre, a cultural institution
Focuses on the Polish-Jewish heritage of Lublin through arts and education programmes

w: Laid out in the 1820s as a drill ground for military parades, this 35,000-square-metre square has stayed Lublin's default stage for state ceremonies ever since. It has held a listed spot on Poland's Register of Historical Monuments since 1972 - recognition for what was, essentially, a parade ground with staying power.
s: A 1820s parade ground, still the city's main stage
_facts: Also called Lithuanian Square; created in the 1820s for military parades, originally 'Drill Square'
About 35,000 square metres; central site for state ceremonies and events in Lublin
Entered Poland's Register of Historical Monuments on 10 April 1972

w: Built between 1635 and 1644 in the distinctive Lublin Renaissance style, this Carmelite church was funded by a noblewoman whose portrait still hangs inside. Figures of St. Teresa of Avila and St. John of the Cross flank its facade, tying a local architectural style to the Carmelite order's own Spanish founders.
s: A Carmelite church in Lublin's own Renaissance style
_facts: Built 1635-1644, funded by Katarzyna Sanguszkowa
Built in the Lublin Renaissance architectural style
Facade features figures of St. Teresa of Ávila and St. John of the Cross; raised with an adjoining Carmelite abbey

w: Founded in 1914 and given its own building nearly a decade later, this is one of the oldest and largest museums in Eastern Poland - a regional institution that has quietly outlasted empires, wars and every border shift the city has seen since it opened.
s: One of the oldest museums in Eastern Poland
_facts: Created in 1914, received its own building in 1923
One of the oldest and largest museums in Eastern Poland

w: Gothic on the outside and startlingly Byzantine within, this castle chapel hides 15th-century frescoes painted in an Orthodox style almost unheard of in Catholic Poland. A king commissioned Ruthenian painters for his private chapel, and their work has survived inside the castle courtyard for six centuries since.
s: Byzantine frescoes inside a Catholic king's chapel
_facts: Gothic chapel with a Renaissance gable, in Lublin Castle's courtyard
Known for 15th-century frescoes painted in Byzantine/Orthodox style
Unusual survival of Orthodox-style religious art inside Catholic Poland

w: Behind an unassuming name lies one of wartime Lublin's darkest addresses: a Nazi torture centre where interrogations were carried out during the occupation. The building now serves as a museum, its clinical nickname - Pod Zegarem, Under the Clock - standing in stark contrast to what actually happened inside.
s: A Gestapo torture site with a deceptively mild name
_facts: Polish name Pod Zegarem, meaning Under the Clock
Was a Nazi torture centre in Lublin during World War II
Now operates as a museum

w: Tucked inside the historic Pociej Palace, this museum of typography keeps Lublin's old printing trade alive through hands-on demonstrations of historic techniques alongside poetry and art programming - less a static exhibit than a working centre reviving skills machines made obsolete generations ago.
s: A working museum of old-fashioned printing
_facts: Polish name Dom Słów, formerly known as Chamber of Printing
Museum of typography and multimodal education centre in Pociej's Palace
Located at Żmigród 1 Street; focuses on poetry, art and the history of Lublin's printing industry

w: Raised in the late 1820s in a strict Classical style on the ruins of a demolished Carmelite monastery, this town hall has quietly continued doing exactly the job it was built for. It still serves today as the seat of Lublin's city president, two centuries of continuous local governance on one square.
s: Two centuries of city government, on a monastery's old site
_facts: Built 1827-1828 in the Classical architectural style
Built on the former site of a Discalced Carmelite monastery
Still functions as the seat of the President of Lublin
